prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "BOEING CO" (ticker BA), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BA", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: The Boeing Company
result.industry: Commercial aircraft, defense and space, and aviation services
markets: Commercial jetliners (737 MAX narrowbodies; 787, 777/777X and 767 widebodies and freighters)
Military aircraft, helicopters and weapons (F-15, F/A-18, KC-46 tanker, P-8, AH-64 Apache, CH-47 Chinook, MQ-25, T-7)
Space and satellites (commercial and government satellites, SLS core stage, Starliner, ULA stake)
Aftermarket services (spare parts, maintenance, modifications, training and government sustainment)

mission.plain: Boeing wants to build the planes, spacecraft and defense systems that connect and protect people, with safety, quality and integrity as its core values.

about.plain: Boeing designs and builds big passenger jets like the 737 and 787 that airlines use to fly people around the world. It also makes military planes, helicopters, satellites and space vehicles for the US government and its allies. After planes are sold, Boeing earns money selling spare parts, fixing and upgrading them, and training crews. It and Airbus are the only two companies that build most of the world's large passenger jets.
about.customers: Airlines, aircraft-leasing companies and cargo carriers, plus the US Department of Defense, NASA and allied governments.
about.everyday: If you have flown on a plane, there is a good chance it was a Boeing 737 or 787; more than 14,000 Boeing airplanes are in service worldwide.

money.plain: passenger jets and freighters (737, 787, 777, 767); $41.5B of 2025 revenue, 600 deliveries
fighters, tankers, helicopters, satellites and space systems; $27.2B of 2025 revenue
spare parts, maintenance, upgrades and training; $20.9B of 2025 revenue and the most profitable unit
the new 777-9 long-haul jet, first delivery expected in 2027
the US Air Force's sixth-generation fighter (NGAD) awarded in 2025, plus the MQ-28 drone wingman

result.summary: Boeing has a real but damaged moat: it is one of only two makers of large passenger jets (with Airbus), with a backlog of $715B at June 30, 2026, decades of certification know-how and a huge installed base that feeds a profitable services business. However, the 2018-2019 737 MAX crashes, the January 2024 door-plug blowout, FAA production caps and years of losses (operating losses in five of the six years 2020-2025) have cost it market share to Airbus and pricing leverage, so the advantage depends on its ongoing quality and production recovery.

pricingPower.evidence: The duopoly and multi-year sold-out order books (gross orders of 1,167 airplanes in 2025, backlog of 6,713 aircraft) support pricing, but Boeing's gross margin (revenue less cost of products and services) was only 4.8% in 2025 and Commercial Airplanes lost $7.1B, reflecting fixed-price contracts, heavy discounting of past MAX and 787 deals and losses on fixed-price defense programs such as KC-46 and T-7.

moats.evidence: Boeing is a globally known aviation brand with a century of history and type certificates for the 737, 767, 777 and 787, but the MAX crashes and the 2024 Alaska Airlines door-plug incident have hurt its safety reputation.

Airlines that standardise on the 737 or 787 share pilot type ratings, spare parts, tooling and maintenance training across the fleet, so switching to Airbus is costly and slow; defense customers depend on Boeing for decades of sustainment.
A larger installed fleet (14,000+ airplanes) deepens the parts, pilot and MRO ecosystem, an indirect benefit rather than a true network effect.

Only Boeing and Airbus have the scale to spread $10B+ new-aircraft development costs over thousands of units, but Boeing currently produces fewer jets than Airbus (600 vs 793 deliveries in 2025) and has absorbed abnormal production costs.

The large-jet market supports only two profitable players; China's COMAC C919 and Embraer have not broken the Boeing-Airbus duopoly, and new entrants need decades and tens of billions of dollars to certify an aircraft.
Boeing is the incumbent and has no business model that rivals cannot copy.

Decades of aircraft design, certification and high-rate assembly know-how are hard to copy, though quality-control lapses since 2019 show this process power has eroded and is being rebuilt, including by bringing Spirit AeroSystems in-house in December 2025.
Its FAA type certificates, classified defense programs (F-47, B-52 upgrades) and specialised engineering workforce (SPEEA-represented engineers) are scarce assets competitors cannot easily obtain.

customers.evidence: Airlines keep ordering (1,167 gross orders in 2025, a large Avolon follow-on order for 140 MAX jets in 2026) because Airbus is sold out for years, but customers such as Ryanair, United and Alaska have publicly criticised delivery delays and quality, and no public NPS is disclosed.

talent.evidence: With about 182,000 employees Boeing is a major aerospace employer, but it has faced a 53-day IAM machinist strike in 2024 and an engineering contract rejected in August 2026 before SPEEA ratified a four-year deal on October 1, 2026 (10% raise up front), and its reputation as an employer has weakened since 2019.

product.evidence: The 787 is a leading efficient widebody and the 777 dominates large freighters (Boeing says its freighters serve more than 90% of global air-freight capacity), but the 737 MAX trails the Airbus A321neo in the largest narrowbody segment and the 737-7, 737-10 and 777X are years late.

competitors.name: Airbus SE
competitors.note: The other half of the large-jet duopoly: A320neo family vs 737 MAX, A350/A330 vs 787/777; also defense and space.

competitors.name: Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (COMAC)
competitors.note: State-owned maker of the C919 narrowbody, a long-term challenger in China and friendly markets.

competitors.name: Embraer S.A.
competitors.note: E-Jet E2 regional jets at the small end of the 737 market; KC-390 military transport.

competitors.name: Lockheed Martin Corporation
competitors.note: Fighters (F-35 vs F-15EX/F/A-18), helicopters (Sikorsky vs Apache/Chinook), space and missiles.

competitors.name: Northrop Grumman Corporation
competitors.note: Military aircraft (B-21), space systems, satellites and missile defense.

competitors.name: RTX Corporation
competitors.note: Missiles and defense electronics (Raytheon) and aftermarket parts/services (Collins, Pratt & Whitney), also a key Boeing supplier.

competitors.name: General Dynamics Corporation
competitors.note: Defense contracts and Gulfstream business jets (vs Boeing Business Jets).

competitors.name: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (SpaceX)
competitors.note: Private; crew and cargo launches (Dragon vs Starliner), satellites and NASA contracts.

competitors.name: Textron Inc. (Bell)
competitors.note: Military rotorcraft (Bell V-280 won the Army's FLRAA program), V-22 partner with Boeing.

competitors.name: L3Harris Technologies, Inc.
competitors.note: Defense electronics, ISR aircraft modifications and space systems.

competitors.name: BAE Systems plc
competitors.note: Military aircraft, electronics and sustainment in the US and allied markets.

competitors.name: Lufthansa Technik AG
competitors.note: Subsidiary of Lufthansa; aircraft maintenance and components services competing with Global Services.

estimates.name: Airbus SE (estimate, converted from EUR 73.4B at about 1.13 USD/EUR)

marketShare.market: Large commercial jet deliveries (Boeing and Airbus combined)
Large commercial jet gross orders (Boeing and Airbus combined)

threats: Further quality or safety lapses that bring back FAA production caps or more groundings of the 737 MAX
Continued delays to 777X, 737-7 and 737-10 certification (777-9 ETOPS testing may slip into 2027 because of a GE9X seal issue)
Airbus extending its lead with the A321neo and its higher production rates, and COMAC's C919 gaining share in China
Losses on fixed-price defense development contracts (KC-46, T-7, MQ-25, VC-25B) and an over-stretched balance sheet ($45.9B of debt, equity of only $6.1B at June 30, 2026)
Labor disruptions (2024 IAM strike; 2026 SPEEA negotiations) and supply-chain bottlenecks in engines and aerostructures
Trade tensions and tariffs affecting orders from China and costs of imported parts

ceo.name: Robert K. (Kelly) Ortberg
ceo.background: Mechanical engineer (University of Iowa); former CEO of Rockwell Collins and senior executive at RTX

c1.evidence: Commercial aviation is a century-old, mature duopoly growing mid-single digits a year, not an emerging industry, and Boeing is currently No. 2 to Airbus in deliveries (600 vs 793 in 2025).

c2.evidence: Airlines choose Boeing for fleet commonality, the 787's efficiency and because Airbus is sold out for years, and the duopoly is very hard to copy, but its reputation for quality has been badly damaged since the 737 MAX crashes.

c3.evidence: Almost everyone recognises the Boeing name and it is one of two default jetliner makers, but surveys and media coverage since 2019 show many travellers are wary of its planes, so it is not a product most would actively recommend today.

c4.evidence: Boeing stresses 'safety, quality and integrity' and a safety and quality plan under Kelly Ortberg, but it publishes no distinctive mission, and its recent history is associated with cost-cutting and shareholder returns rather than purpose.

c6.evidence: "airplanes, troubled, safety concerns, American icon" - the impression is mixed to negative today, as respect for its engineering heritage is offset by the MAX crashes and the 2024 door-plug blowout.

c7.evidence: Air travel and fleet replacement give a large, growing market (Boeing's backlog was $715B at June 30, 2026), helped by rising defense spending, though it grows at mid-single digits rather than like AI or cloud.

c8.evidence: Boeing can grow in services, autonomous aircraft (MQ-25, MQ-28), the F-47 sixth-generation fighter and space, but these are extensions of aerospace rather than big new markets.

m1.evidence: Kelly Ortberg has a clear plan to stabilise production and rebuild culture, but his vision is a turnaround rather than a bold picture of the future.

m2.evidence: Ortberg is a hired CEO, not a founder, but he moved to Seattle to be close to the factories and focuses on long-term fixes such as buying Spirit AeroSystems back.

m4.evidence: Ortberg has emphasised walking the factory floor and resetting relations with workers, including the 2024 IAM settlement and the October 2026 SPEEA deal, though labor relations remain tense.

m5.evidence: He is trying to rebuild an engineering and quality culture after years of criticism, but Boeing has not launched a clean-sheet airliner since the 787 (2011).

m6.evidence: Ortberg is a mechanical engineer who spent his career in aerospace engineering and operations at Rockwell Collins.

m7.evidence: Ortberg is regarded as a steady, credible leader focused on safety, but there is not enough public evidence to judge his character beyond his conduct of the turnaround.

m7b.evidence: There is no record of Kelly Ortberg giving a commencement speech at a top university such as Stanford, Harvard or MIT.

m8b.evidence: Ortberg is known as a low-key, plain-spoken engineer rather than a celebrity CEO.

m9.evidence: He built a strong record at Rockwell Collins and since August 2024 has lifted deliveries to 600 in 2025 and 475 in the first nine months of 2026, but Boeing still lost money in the first half of 2026.

m10.evidence: Boeing is not known for frugality, and its past cost-cutting focus is widely blamed for its quality problems rather than seen as a virtue.

c10.evidence: Boeing airplanes carry a large share of the world's air travellers and freight (its freighters serve more than 90% of global air-cargo capacity, according to Boeing).

p2.evidence: Designing and certifying a jetliner takes about a decade and tens of billions of dollars, which is why only two Western companies can do it at scale.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose from $58.2B in 2020 to $62.3B, $66.6B and $77.8B, fell to $66.5B in 2024 (strike and FAA cap), then rose to $89.5B in 2025, so it grew in four of the last five years.

f2.evidence: Operating margin improved from -22.0% in 2020 to 4.8% in 2025, but 2025 included a $9.6B gain on selling Digital Aviation Solutions and margins remain far below Boeing's pre-2019 levels.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 Boeing had $45.9B of debt against $20.0B of cash and investments and only $6.1B of shareholders' equity, with 2025 operating cash flow of just $1.1B.

f4.evidence: Operating income improved from -$12.8B in 2020 to $4.3B in 2025 and operating cash flow from -$18.4B to $1.1B, but both swung sharply negative in 2024 (-$10.7B and -$12.1B).

v1.evidence: The 787 is a strong widebody, but in the biggest segment the Airbus A321neo outsells and outranges the 737 MAX, so Boeing is not clearly best.

v2.evidence: Boeing has not featured near the top of recent 'best places to work' rankings, and engineers rejected a contract offer in August 2026 before ratifying a new one in October.

c5.evidence: Airlines, cargo carriers and the US and allied militaries would be badly affected if Boeing disappeared, because Airbus could not build enough planes to replace its roughly 600 deliveries a year.
